The legislature is free to legislate on topics and subjects carved out for it. Similarly,
the executive is free to implement and administer the law. A law made by a
legislature may be bad or may be ultra vires, but since it is an exercise of legislative
power, a person affected by it may challenge its validity but he cannot approach a
court of law for negligence in making the law. Nor can the Government in exercise of
its executive action be sued for its decision on political or policy matters. It is in
public interest that for acts performed by the State either in its legislative or executive
capacity it should not be answerable in torts. That would be illogical and impractical.
It would be in conflict with even modern notions of sovereignty. One of the tests to
determine if the legislative or executive function is sovereign in nature is whether the
State is answerable for such actions in courts of law. For instance, acts such as
defence of the country, raising armed forces and maintaining it, making peace or war,
foreign affairs, power to acquire and retain territory, are functions which are
indicative of external sovereignty and are political in nature. Therefore, they are not
amenable to jurisdiction of ordinary civil court. No suit under Civil Procedure Code
would lie in respect of it. The State is immune from being sued, as the jurisdiction of
the courts in such matter is impliedly barred.
25. But there the immunity ends. No civilised system can permit an executive to play
with the people of its country and claim that it is entitled to act in any manner as it is
sovereign. The concept of public interest has changed with structural change in the
society. No legal or political system today can place the State above law as it is unjust
and unfair for a citizen to be deprived Page No.# 74/97 of his property illegally by
negligent act of officers of the State without any remedy. From sincerity, efficiency
and dignity of State as a juristic person, propounded in nineteenth century as sound
sociological basis for State immunity the circle has gone round and the emphasis now
is more on liberty, equality and the rule of law. The modern social thinking of
progressive societies and the judicial approach is to do away with archaic State
protection and place the State or the Government on a par with any other juristic
legal entity. Any watertight compartmentalization of the functions of the State as
"sovereign and non-sovereign" or "governmental and non-governmental" is not
sound. It is contrary to modern jurisprudential thinking. The need of the State to
have extraordinary powers cannot be doubted. But with the conceptual change of
statutory power being statutory duty for sake of society and the people the claim of a
common man or ordinary citizen cannot be thrown out merely because it was done by
an officer of the State even though it was against law and negligent. Needs of the
State, duty of its officials and right of the citizens are required to be reconciled so that
the rule of law in a Welfare State is not shaken. Even in America where this doctrine
of sovereignty found its place either because of the "financial instability of the infant
American States rather than to the stability of the doctrine's theoretical foundation",
or because of "logical and practical ground", or that "there could be no legal right as
against the State which made the law" gradually gave way to the movement from,
"State irresponsibility to State responsibility". In Welfare State, functions of the State
are not only defence of the country or administration of justice or maintaining law

generally time-consuming and expensive, and hence when fundamental rights are violated the
claimants prefer to approach constitutional courts for speedy remedy. The constitutional courts, of

Constitutional torts and punitive damages
104. Constitutional courts' actions not only strive to compensate the victims and vindicate their
constitutional rights, but also to deter future constitutional misconduct without proper excuse or
with some collateral or improper motive. The constitutional Page No.# 85/97 courts can in
appropriate cases of serious violation of life and liberty of the individuals award punitive damages.
However, the same generally requires the presence of malicious intent on the side of the wrongdoer
i.e. an intentional doing of some wrongful act.
105. Compensatory damages are intended to provide the claimant with a monetary amount
necessary to recoup/replace what was lost, since damages in tort are generally awarded to place the
claimants in the position he would have been in, had the tort not taken place; which are generally
quantified under the heads of general damages and special damages. Punitive damages are intended
to reform or to deter the wrongdoer from indulging in conduct similar to that which formed the
basis for the claim. Punitive damages are not intended to compensate the claimant which he can
claim in an ordinary private law claim in tort. Punitive damages are awarded by the constitutional
court when the wrongdoer's conduct was egregiously deceitful.
108. Several factors may gauge on a constitutional court in determining the punitive damages such
as contumacious conduct of the wrongdoer, the nature of the statute, gravity of the fault committed,
the circumstances, etc. Punitive damages can be awarded when the wrongdoers' conduct "shocks the
conscience" or is "outrageous" or there is a wilful and "wanton disregard" for safety requirements.
Normally, there must be a direct connection between the wrongdoer's conduct and the victim's

"14. Once we come to a conclusion that Sunil is killed in an encounter, which appears

peculiar facts and circumstances, and striking and disconcerting features obtaining in the present

112.1 The fact remains that these two deceased were in the prime of their lives in their early twenties
and one of them was educated. Both of them were hale and hearty when they were picked up by
army personnel. They were not armed when they were picked by the army personnel.
112.2 They were in the custody of the army for 2-3 days before they were killed. Keeping any person
in custody by the army for such a prolonged period even if suspected of being a member of an
insurgent group without handing them over to the civil police and Magistrate is against the mandate
of law as held in Sebestian M. Hongray (supra) (1984). In the present case, they were kept in
custody for 2-3 days without any authority of law after they were apprehended.
112.3 It is not a case of accidental death caused on being caught in the cross firing between the

112.4 It is not a case of death which occurred on the spur of the moment during an Page No.# 94/97
encounter. There was no encounter. It was a planned execution. They were already in the custody of
the army authorities for fairly a long period of time and were subjected to torture and thereafter,
killed in cold blood as clearly revealed in the Inquiry Report. They thus, suffered an undeserved
violent death.

an unwarranted manner without any cogent reason which would only lead to the inevitable
conclusion that these two persons had met an untimely, unwarranted, undeserved violent death at

the yeoman service rendered by the valiant Indian army and the security forces especially in this
part of the country, in upholding the integrity of our country and in maintaining peace and

The present petition has been filed by 2(two) petitioners, namely, Sri Konto Warisa and Sri Golom Nunisa who alleged that their sons, namely, Poresh Warisa and Sujit Nunisa, aged about 23 years, residents of Wari Lamphu village were picked up by the personnel of 12th Battalion Madras Regiment on 14.07.2009 from the said village and subsequently, were shot dead and the dead bodies brought to the Haflong Police Station on 19.07.2009. The said Poresh Warisa has been also referred to as Pirush Warisa, and sometimes as Pirosh Warisa and Phirosh Warisa in the pleadings.

In connection with an incident, an F.I.R. was lodged with the Dehangi Police Station by Dimanon Kemprai. Dehangi P.S. Case No. 05/2009 dated 20.07.2009 was registered under Section 302 IPC against the personnel of the 12th Battalion Madras Regiment. The petition seeks a direction for holding a judicial inquiry into the killing of Poresh Warisa and Sujit Nunisa and to take appropriate action against the army personnel. The petition has been contested by the respondents alleging that the two persons were killed in an encounter when they hurled grenades and started firing indiscriminately.

Captain James Jacob of 12th Battalion, Madras Regiment and his team conducted an operation at Wari Lampu village from the early hours of 14.07.2009. Both Poresh Warisa and Sujit Nunisa, residents of Wari Lampu village, did not have any criminal background and were not connected with any extremist outfit like DHD-J. They were young, healthy, and able-bodied individuals. They were tortured by the personnel of 12th Battalion, Madras Regiment, which made them very weak and infirm. They were then taken from Wari Lampu village to Dimadao Wapo village by tying them on two bamboo poles. The story of Madras Regiment that one of the two Dimasa youths first hurled one grenade which blasted and thereafter both of them fired at the party of 12th Battalion, Madras Regiment is not believable as both the youths were cordoned and surrounded by the team of about 30 personnel of 12th Battalion, Madras Regiment. Sepoy Yellapa Goudra was treated at Haflong Civil Hospital on 18.07.2009 at 05:30 pm as per the Medical Examination Report (Ext.3) of Dr. Lalawmilan Suantak which was proved by PW8 Dr. Parikshit Barman. The inquiry report found that the personnel of the Madras Regiment had conducted an operation at Wari Lamphu village from early hours of 14.07.2009 without involving the civil administration or the police in which the aforesaid two persons were tortured and subsequently killed.

On 14 June 2009, 12 Madras Regiment received information regarding the presence of DHD(J) cadres in villages Wari Lampu and Dimadao. On 16 July 2009, an individual named Perush Warisa was detained while trying to escape the cordon. He confessed to being an OWG'S and revealed the presence of other DHD(J) members. Assam Police was requisitioned and apprehended two female cadres. On 17 July 2009, six more female cadres were apprehended and handed over to Haflong Police Station. On 18 July 2009, Sujith Nunisa was detained and revealed the location of weapons hidden in the jungle near New Sangbar.

On 14.07.2009, an Army party of 12th Madras Regiment arrived at Warilampu village and asked about the movement of extremists. They assaulted the complainant's nephew and grandson, Phirosh Warisa and Sujit Nunisa, and tortured them by electric shock. The Army party conducted operations for three consecutive days and took the villagers away. On 19.07.2009, the complainant learned that Phirosh Warisa and Sujit Nunisa had died and their bodies were sent to Haflong Civil Hospital for post-mortem examination. The FIR was lodged on 20.07.2009.

On 14/07/09, the 12th Bn. Madras Regiment launched an operation based on specific information about the presence of hard core DHD(J) cadres at Warilampu village under Dehangi P.S. They apprehended DHD cadre Sujit Nunisa and Perush Warisa. During interrogation, they learned that weapons were hidden in the jungle. An operation was launched on 18.07.2009, resulting in a confrontation where both cadres were killed, and one Army sepoy, Yellappa Goudra, sustained a bullet injury.

Witnesses from Warilangpo village, P.S.- Dehangi, stated that on 14/07/2009 at 4:30 AM, the Army cordoned the village and brought all males and females to the local Gaonburah's house. The deceased were also brought there and allegedly tortured. On 17/07/2009, the Army took away several individuals including Sujit Nunisha and Perush Warisha, who could not walk due to torture. The Army then took six people, handing over four to Haflong PS on 18/07/2009, and the remaining two were killed in a so-called encounter. The doctors who conducted the post-mortem examinations noted multiple injuries besides bullet wounds, suggesting physical torture.

This Court after perusal of the status report submitted by CID (Assam) in the light of the averments made in the writ petition as well as the counter claim made in the affidavit-in-oppositions, more particularly of the respondent Nos.1 and 2, was of the opinion that an inquiry be conducted by the learned District & Sessions Judge, Dima Hasao, Haflong, to inquire into the circumstances leading to the death of two detenues, namely, Poresh Warisa and Sujit Nunisa, relating which Dehangi P.S. Case No.05/2009 dated 20.07.2009 under Section 302 IPC was registered. It was directed that the inquiry be completed within 4(four) months. Subsequently, on completion of the inquiry, the Inquiry Report dt. 23.02.2021 was submitted before this Court and this Court furnished copies of the inquiry report to all the respondents and thereafter the matter was heard. Mr. Hazarika, learned counsel for the petitioners, based on the inquiry report, submitted that both the deceased, Poresh Warisa and Sujit Nunisa, were killed in cold blood by the personnel of 12th Battalion, Madras Regiment after they were taken into custody and subjected to torture by them on 14.07.2009. He further submitted that the aforesaid two persons did not have any criminal background and there was no record to indicate their involvement with any of the extremist outfits like DHD(J). The version of the army that both of them died in retaliatory fire after they tried to escape from the custody of the army by hurling grenade, has not been established in course of inquiry and thus, rejected by the learned District and Sessions Judge. The petitioners claim that the respondent authorities should be liable to pay compensation at least to the tune of Rs.20,00,000/- (Rupees twenty lakhs) each to the petitioners.

texts.reasoning_text:
This Court directed the District and Sessions Judge, Dima Hasao, Haflong to conduct a judicial inquiry to ascertain the circumstances leading to the death of the two detenues. The inquiry was conducted by examining 9 witnesses in support of the claim of the petitioners, 2 court witnesses, and 2 witnesses examined by the respondents. Post-mortem reports, injury reports, and general diaries were also examined.

While considering the Inquiry Report, the Court clarified that it was not sitting as an appellate court. The inquiry was directed to be conducted by this Court in order to satisfy itself of the veracity of the claims made by the petitioners in the light of the contradictory version by the army authorities and for the purpose of appropriate relief that may be granted by this Court. The inquiry was not akin to any criminal trial nor a criminal investigation, but to ascertain the circumstances under which the aforesaid two deceased had

The court clarified that the inquiry proceeding before the District and Sessions Judge is not a criminal trial but an inquiry to ascertain the bases for the allegations of custodial torture and death of the two petitioners at the hands of the army personnel. The persuasive value of the Inquiry Report will be examined by applying the principle of preponderance of probability.

The ballistic expert, Sri Upen Borah, agreed with the post-mortem reports indicating the deceased died due to bullet injuries. He noted the short time frame for a grenade to explode and the improbability of no Army personnel being injured by grenade splinters.

The court notes that the army authorities' version of events is inconsistent with their own records and pleadings. For instance, the affidavit in opposition filed by the respondents No. 1 and 2 differs from the testimony of DW 1 regarding the apprehension of Pirush Warisa and Sujit Nunisa. These inconsistencies render the version of the army authorities unreliable.

The court notes that the army did not adhere to the norms as required under the law. It emphasizes the importance of involving civil authorities and the police in such operations and highlights the need to follow the 'Dos and Don'ts' list issued by the Army Headquarters.

The non-involvement of the police by the army personnel at the most crucial part of the operation, in the light of the aforesaid mandatory Dos and Don'ts, is incomprehensible. There is no reliable evidence to show that the deceased were involved with the activities of the extremist outfit.

The court considers the testimonies of PW1 to PW7 and the medical evidence from post-mortem reports. The court also notes the testimony of CW2, Sri Upen Bora, and the account of DW2 regarding the presence of 30 army personnel surrounding the two deceased persons.

The court notes that the operation was conducted during broad daylight, making it unlikely that the grenade and arms were found on the ground without being noticed by the surrounding army personnel. The court also considers the evidence of CW2, who stated that it is highly improbable that not a single army personnel was injured by the splinters on the blasting of the grenade.

The court observed that the army authorities had the burden and onus to prove that the recovery of arms and ammunitions were at the instance of the two deceased persons. The court noted that the police did not believe the version of the army as clearly mentioned in the status report submitted before the Court. The court found no reason not to accept the conclusion that hurling of grenade and firing by the two deceased is not believable.

The court notes that the contemporaneous medical report from Haflong Civil Hospital indicates a simple injury without any deep structure damage, contradicting the claim of a gunshot wound. The lack of mention of severe injury or loss of consciousness in earlier affidavits raises doubts about the authenticity of the claimed gunshot injury.

The burden of proving the circumstances under which the two persons died is on the army authorities, as the events are especially within their knowledge. The army authorities have failed to satisfactorily explain the death of the two persons in their custody and how they received multiple injuries over their bodies.

The court notes that the inquiry was focused and the army authorities had the opportunity to call additional witnesses but chose not to. The court finds that the army authorities failed to provide satisfactory explanations for the bruises on the deceased and the alleged injury of Yellappa Goudra. The court also finds that the recovery of arms and ammunition alone does not prove the deceased were militants.

The court can certainly injunct the State from depriving a person of his life or personal liberty except in accordance with procedure established by law, but if life or personal liberty is violated otherwise than in accordance with such procedure, is the court helpless to grant relief to the person who has suffered such deprivation?

We see no effective answer to the argument that the State must pay compensation for the gross violation of the petitioner's fundamental right to liberty. The right to compensation is some palliative for the unlawful acts of instrumentalities which act in the name of public interest and which present for their protection the powers of the State as a shield.

That the said law is now firmly entranced in our jurisprudence, can be seen from the later judgment in Nilabati Behera Vs. State of Orissa, (1993) 2 SCC 746 which exposited the law in very clear terms as follows: In Rudul Sah [(1983) 4 SCC 141 : 1983 SCC (Cri) 798 : (1983) 3 SCR 508] it was held that in a petition under Article 32 of the Constitution, this Court can grant compensation for deprivation of a fundamental right. That was a case of violation of the petitioner's right to personal liberty under Article 21 of the Constitution.

The Court allowed the petition and directed appropriate actions against the erring army personnel and awarded adequate compensation to the families of the deceased.

Taking into consideration the great harm done to the petitioner by the Government of Bihar, we are of the opinion that, as an interim measure, the State must pay to the petitioner a further sum of Rs 30,000 (Rupees thirty thousand) in addition to the sum of Rs 5000 (Rupees five thousand) already paid by it.

The Court has determined that there is no consistent view regarding the quantum of compensation for violation of fundamental rights, and there is a need for uniform principles to determine compensation amounts.

With the above observations and directions, we allow this petition.

Both Poresh Warisa and Sujit Nunisa, residents of Wari Lampu village, did not have any criminal background and were not connected with any extremist outfit like DHD-J.
